Wisconsin law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there.

What the official sources say

  • Adverse possession not founded on a written instrument: 20 years of uninterrupted adverse possession bars an owner's action for recovery of possession. (Wis. Stat. 893.25(1); source)
  • Possession is adverse under 893.25 only if the possessor is in actual continued occupation under claim of title, exclusive of any other right, and the land is protected by a substantial enclosure or usually cultivated or improved. (Wis. Stat. 893.25(2); source)
  • A 7-year period applies where the possessor meets the 10-year requirements and also pays all real estate taxes for the 7 years after original entry. (Wis. Stat. 893.27(1), (2)(b); source)
  • Landlord may hold personal property left by a trespasser removed from residential rental property for 7 days before disposing of it. (Wis. Stat. 704.055(2)(a); source)

Wisconsin Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Landlord may enter only upon advance notice and at reasonable times; advance notice means at least 12 hours unless the tenant consents to shorter. Exceptions: tenant consent, health or safety emergency, tenant absent and entry needed to protect premises. (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP 134.09(2); source)
  • Landlord duties: keep portions under its control and service equipment in reasonable repair, make necessary structural repairs, and for residential tenancies comply with local housing code. (Wis. Stat. 704.07(2)(a); source)
  • If premises are untenantable or there is a substantial violation materially affecting health or safety, tenant may move out unless landlord promptly repairs; if tenant stays, rent abates, but rent may not be withheld in full. Residential waiver of this section is void. (Wis. Stat. 704.07(1), (4); source)

What laws govern landlords and tenants in Wisconsin?

Two bodies of law do most of the work: chapter 704 of the Wisconsin Statutes and chapter ATCP 134 of the Administrative Code. Chapter 704 covers repairs, notices to end a tenancy, security deposits and the effect of a transfer. Chapter ATCP 134, administered by the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection, sets residential rental practices.

Chapter ATCP 134 applies to dwelling units in the state. It excludes a short list, including units run by institutions, units occupied under a contract of sale, tourist or transient stays under 60 days, and units owned and run by a government. A tenant who loses money because of a violation can sue directly and recover twice the loss plus costs and attorney fees.

If you are selling a rental, these rules decide what the buyer inherits, how much time you must give a tenant, and what you owe back from a deposit.

What happens to a lease when a Wisconsin landlord sells the property?

The lease generally stays in place. Wis. Stat. 704.09 says a landlord's interest may be transferred unless the lease expressly restricts that power, and a restriction is read to cover voluntary transfers unless it also names transfers by operation of law.

  • Covenants in the lease that are not personal to the original parties can be enforced by or against the successor.
  • A successor is liable in damages only for breaches that happen while the successor holds the interest, unless the successor agrees to more by contract.
  • The seller stays on the hook for the lease obligations unless the lease or an express release says otherwise.
  • The remedies available between the original landlord and tenant are also available to or against a successor.

A cash buyer who takes a rented house therefore steps into the lease. Give the buyer a copy of each lease and a ledger of rent and deposits.

How much notice does a Wisconsin landlord have to give before ending a tenancy?

The notice period depends on the type of tenancy and the reason. The shortest common notice is 5 days for unpaid rent, and a periodic tenancy needs 28 days of written notice to end without cause.

SituationNoticeSource
Month-to-month or week-to-week, unpaid rentPay or vacate on a date at least 5 days after noticeWis. Stat. 704.17(1p)(a)
Month-to-month tenant in default on rentVacate notice at least 14 days after givingWis. Stat. 704.17(1p)(a)
Lease of one year or less, unpaid rentPay or vacate at least 5 days after notice; 14 days if repeated within one yearWis. Stat. 704.17(2)(a)
Lease of one year or less, other breachRemedy or vacate at least 5 days after noticeWis. Stat. 704.17(2)(b)
Lease of more than one yearAt least 30 days to pay, repair or complyWis. Stat. 704.17(3)(a)
Criminal activity threatening othersVacate at least 5 days after notice, no chance to remedyWis. Stat. 704.17(3m)(b)
Periodic tenancy, no causeAt least 28 days of written notice, ending at the end of a rental periodWis. Stat. 704.19(2), (3)

The text is in Wis. Stat. 704.17 and 704.19. Notice is counted from the day it is given, and mailed notice is treated as given on the 2nd day after mailing within the state. For a breach other than rent, a tenant is treated as complying with the notice if they promptly take reasonable steps to fix the problem.

How does a Wisconsin eviction work after the notice runs out?

The landlord files an eviction action in court, and a judgment is followed by a writ of restitution that the sheriff carries out. Wis. Stat. 799.40 lets the person entitled to possession, or an agent authorized in writing, start the case.

  • Proof of certified mailing from the post office is enough to show a termination notice was properly given, and no affidavit of service can be demanded.
  • A landlord who accepts past due rent after serving notice or filing the case does not lose the action for that reason.
  • If the court finds the plaintiff entitled to possession, it orders judgment and orders a writ of restitution to issue right away.
  • The writ cannot be carried out if the sheriff receives it more than 30 days after it was issued.
  • A court that sees hardship can stay the writ for up to 30 days, on the condition that the tenant pays unpaid rent and the reasonable value of occupancy.

The sheriff may require a deposit toward removal costs under s. 799.45(1) unless the landlord tells the sheriff that the landlord will remove and store or dispose of the property.

What if a tenant leaves belongings behind?

Under Wis. Stat. 704.05(5), a landlord may presume that property left behind by a departed or evicted tenant is abandoned, and may dispose of it as the landlord decides, unless the written agreement says otherwise.

  • Prescription medication and prescription medical equipment must be held for 7 days, and returned promptly if the tenant asks before disposal.
  • A manufactured home, mobile home or titled vehicle needs written notice of intent to dispose to the tenant and to any secured party the landlord knows about.
  • A landlord who does not plan to store belongings must give written notice of that when the tenant signs or renews a lease.
  • The tenant or a secured party can redeem the property before disposal by paying the landlord's expenses.

What repair and entry duties does a Wisconsin landlord have?

A landlord must keep the parts of the premises under the landlord's control in reasonable repair and make necessary structural repairs. For a residential tenancy the landlord must also follow the local housing code. These duties come from s. 704.07(2), and a lease clause that waives them is void.

If a residential unit becomes untenantable or has a substantial violation that materially affects health or safety, the tenant may move out unless the landlord promptly repairs. A tenant who stays has rent reduced to the extent of lost use, but cannot withhold rent in full.

On entry, ATCP 134.09(2) allows entry during a tenancy only to inspect, make repairs, or show the unit to prospective tenants or purchasers. The landlord must give at least 12 hours of advance notice and enter at reasonable times unless the tenant consents to a shorter time or is absent and the landlord reasonably believes entry is needed to protect the premises. The landlord must announce before entering. A seller who wants showings should plan around that notice window.

When must a Wisconsin landlord return a security deposit?

A residential landlord must deliver or mail the deposit, less lawful deductions, within 21 days after the tenancy ends. Wis. Stat. 704.28(4) counts the 21 days from the lease termination date if the tenant leaves on that date, from the date a new tenant begins if the unit is re-rented early, or from the day the landlord learns the tenant has left.

Standard deductions cover tenant damage, waste or neglect, unpaid rent, and certain unpaid utility charges. A landlord can add other deductions only through a separate written document titled "Nonstandard Rental Provisions" that is identified to the tenant before signing. ATCP 134.06 also bars a landlord from falsifying a claim against a deposit.

When a house sells, the deposit ledger should travel with the lease. Ask the buyer in writing to acknowledge the deposit amounts.

More questions about Wisconsin Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

How many days notice must a Wisconsin landlord give to end a month-to-month tenancy?

At least 28 days of written notice, ending at the end of a rental period, under Wis. Stat. 704.19. For unpaid rent, a month-to-month landlord can give a pay-or-vacate notice with a date at least 5 days after the notice is given.

Does a tenant have to leave when the landlord sells?

No. A sale does not end a lease on its own. Under Wis. Stat. 704.09, the landlord's interest transfers to the buyer, and covenants not personal to the original parties bind the successor.

How long does a landlord have to return a security deposit?

The landlord must deliver or mail it within 21 days, counted from the lease end, the start of a replacement tenancy, or the day the landlord learns the tenant moved out, depending on the facts in s. 704.28(4).

How much notice must a landlord give before entering a rental?

At least 12 hours of advance notice, at reasonable times, unless the tenant agrees to a shorter period. ATCP 134.09(2) limits entry to inspections, repairs and showings to prospective tenants or purchasers, with limited exceptions.

Can a tenant withhold all rent for bad conditions?

No. Wis. Stat. 704.07(4) lets a tenant move out for untenantable conditions or reduce rent in proportion to lost use, but it does not authorize withholding rent in full while the tenant stays.

Wisconsin Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Other breach/waste: 14-day notice to vacate where the tenant repeats within one year after a prior notice; 14-day notice to vacate also appears for month-to-month tenants who breach. (Wis. Stat. 704.17; source)
  • Eviction is a small claims action in circuit court; on judgment for restitution the court orders a writ of restitution issued, delivered to the sheriff, who must execute it within 10 days of receipt; a writ is not executed if received by the sheriff more than 30 days after issuance. (Wis. Stat. 799.44(2), 799.45(5)(a); source)
  • The sheriff removes the defendant and persons claiming under the defendant using reasonable force. (Wis. Stat. 799.45(2)(a); source)
Selling in Wisconsin?
We buy Wisconsin houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What eviction notice does a Wisconsin landlord have to give?

The notice depends on the type of tenancy and the reason for ending it. Under Wis. Stat. 704.17, a tenant who misses rent gets a notice of at least 5 days if the tenancy is month-to-month, week-to-week, or a lease of one year or less, and at least 30 days if the lease runs longer than a year. The table below lays out the main Wisconsin notices.

SituationNotice lengthStatute
Unpaid rent, month-to-month or week-to-weekPay or vacate at least 5 days out. A month-to-month tenant in default can instead get a vacate notice at least 14 days out.704.17(1p)(a)
Unpaid rent, lease of one year or less, or year-to-yearPay or vacate at least 5 days out. A second default within one year allows a 14-day vacate notice.704.17(2)(a)
Other breach or waste, month-to-monthRemedy or vacate at least 5 days out, or a 14-day vacate notice704.17(1p)(b)
Other breach or waste, lease of one year or lessRemedy or vacate at least 5 days out. A repeat within one year allows a 14-day vacate notice.704.17(2)(b)
Any default, lease longer than one yearAt least 30 days to pay, repair or comply704.17(3)(a)
Criminal or drug-related activityVacate at least 5 days out, with no chance to remedy704.17(3m)(b)
No-fault end of a month-to-month tenancyAt least 28 days, ending at the close of a rental period704.19(2), (3)

The statute defines rent to include past due rent and late fees owed for it, so a pay-or-vacate notice can include both.

What does a tenant have to do to cure a Wisconsin notice?

For a breach other than rent, the tenant is treated as complying if, right after receiving the notice, the tenant takes reasonable steps to fix the problem and keeps working on it with reasonable diligence. A tenant also complies when damages protect the landlord and the tenant makes a good-faith, reasonable offer to pay them. Both tests appear in 704.17(1p)(b), (2)(b) and (3)(a).

Rent works differently on a lease longer than a year: all rent due must be paid by the date in the notice. A repeat breach within one year of an earlier notice removes the cure period, and the landlord can give a 14-day notice to vacate instead.

  • Criminal activity that threatens other tenants, neighbors, or the landlord, and drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises, can end a tenancy with a 5-day notice and no cure period.
  • The notice for criminal activity must describe the activity, give the date, identify the people involved, and tell the tenant about the right to contest it in court.
  • A tenant who is the victim of the criminal activity is excluded from that rule under 704.17(3m)(c).
  • Under Wis. Stat. 704.16(3), a landlord can end the tenancy of a tenant whose acts put another tenant in the same building at imminent risk of serious physical harm, with at least 5 days' written notice, when one of the listed court filings or orders exists.

How must a Wisconsin landlord deliver the notice?

The notice must be in writing and delivered by a method listed in Wis. Stat. 704.21. A tenant has no right to stay after the termination date in a properly given notice.

  • Hand it to the tenant, or leave it at the tenant's usual home with a family member at least 14 years old who is told what it says.
  • Leave a copy with a competent person in charge of the premises and mail a copy to the tenant's last-known address.
  • If those methods fail despite reasonable diligence, post it in a conspicuous place on the premises and mail a copy.
  • Send it by registered or certified mail to the tenant's last-known address.
  • Serve it the way a summons is served under Wis. Stat. 801.11.

A notice that misses the listed methods still counts if the tenant actually received it, though the person claiming receipt must prove it by clear and convincing evidence. For a notice sent by certified mail, Wis. Stat. 799.40(1g) makes the post office's proof of mailing enough to show proper notice when the landlord files in court. For 28-day notices, 704.19(7) counts the day of giving as day one, and mail inside Wisconsin is treated as given on the second day after mailing.

Can a Wisconsin lease or a mistake change the notice rules?

A lease cannot shorten these protections except on leases longer than one year. Under 704.17(5), lease terms on termination that conflict with the section are invalid, with that one exception, and any lease term contrary to the criminal activity rule in subsection (3m) is invalid on every lease.

Small errors do not always sink a notice. A rent notice that states the wrong amount is still valid unless the landlord's figure was intentionally wrong or the tenant paid or tendered what the tenant believes is due (704.17(4m)). For a notice ending a periodic tenancy, an error that does not mislead does not void it, and a wrong termination date makes the notice effective on the first proper date after the one stated (704.19(4), (5)).

What happens after the Wisconsin notice period ends?

The landlord has to go to court. A properly given notice ends the tenant's right to occupy, and removal then runs through an eviction action, which Wisconsin handles as a small claims case under chapter 799. The person entitled to possession, or an agent authorized in writing, can start it under Wis. Stat. 799.40(1).

Taking back past due rent after the notice or after filing does not force the court to dismiss the case (799.40(1m)). In an eviction, the summons return date falls 5 to 25 days after the issue date, and the tenant must be served at least 5 days before it (799.05(3)(b)). If the landlord wins, the court orders a writ of restitution and the sheriff executes it under Wis. Stat. 799.44(2) and 799.45.

How does a tenant affect selling a rented house in Wisconsin?

A tenant who is not in default keeps exclusive possession until the lease ends or a periodic tenancy is terminated. Wis. Stat. 704.05(2) adds that the landlord may, on advance notice and at reasonable times, show the premises to prospective purchasers. That default rule applies unless both sides signed a lease provision that says otherwise.

Owners who want the house empty at closing should match the notice to the tenancy before setting a closing date. A no-fault month-to-month notice needs 28 days and must end at the close of a rental period, while a lease longer than a year needs 30 days for a default. Selling with the tenant in place avoids the notice and court steps entirely, and an owner can weigh that against the timeline for removal.

More questions about Wisconsin Eviction Notice Rules

How many days is a Wisconsin eviction notice for unpaid rent?

Five days for a month-to-month, week-to-week, or one-year-or-shorter tenancy, and 30 days for a lease longer than one year. A month-to-month tenant in default can alternatively receive a 14-day vacate notice. The notice must be in writing and delivered by a method in Wis. Stat. 704.21.

Can a Wisconsin landlord evict without giving a chance to fix the problem?

Yes in some cases. A tenant who repeats a breach within one year can get a 14-day vacate notice. Criminal activity that threatens health or safety, and drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises, allow a 5-day notice with no cure period. A tenant who is the victim of the criminal activity is excluded.

How long is the notice to end a month-to-month tenancy with no fault?

At least 28 days, in writing, ending at the close of a rental period. If rent is payable more often than monthly, a notice equal to the rent-paying period is enough. The notice has to say the landlord intends to end the tenancy and give the date.

Does a Wisconsin landlord have to mail the eviction notice?

No. Wis. Stat. 704.21 lists several methods, including handing it to the tenant, leaving it with a family member or person in charge plus mailing, posting plus mailing, certified mail, or service like a summons. Certified mail has a court benefit, because proof of mailing is enough to show notice.

Is a notice enough to remove a tenant in Wisconsin?

No. After the notice period, the landlord must file an eviction action in court. If the landlord wins, the court orders a writ of restitution and the sheriff removes the tenant. The sheriff must execute the writ within 10 days of receiving it.
